title: Keystone species

definition.text: A species whose effect on its surroundings is far larger than its numbers would suggest.

facts.text: The zoologist Robert T. Paine introduced the concept in 1969.
Like the keystone of an arch, it may be a small part of the ecosystem by biomass, yet removing it can trigger a dramatic shift.
When Paine removed ochre starfish from rock pools, mussels took over: 15 clinging species fell to 8 within three years, and ten years later mussels largely filled the pools.
When fur hunting cut sea otters to fewer than 1000 in the north Pacific, sea urchins grazed away the kelp forests; reintroducing otters restored them.
Removing gray wolves from Greater Yellowstone led to overgrazing that hurt beavers and streams; after wolves returned, the riparian ecosystem recovered within a few years.
Keystone mutualists matter through helpful partnerships: some seeds will not grow unless they have passed through a cassowary.
The concept overlaps with flagship, indicator and umbrella species, and has helped ecologists communicate with conservation policymakers.
One researcher listed 230 species called keystones in about 157 studies over the 50 years since Paine's paper.

contested_note: Critics say the term oversimplifies complex ecosystems, has been stretched to many different meanings, and depends on local context.

title: Primary production

definition.text: The making of organic compounds from carbon dioxide in air or water, mainly by photosynthesis.

facts.text: Almost all life on Earth relies directly or indirectly on primary production.
The organisms that do it, called primary producers or autotrophs, form the base of the food chain: mainly plants on land and algae in water.
A small share is driven by chemosynthesis, which takes energy from chemical reactions of inorganic compounds instead of light.
On land it depends mainly on water and temperature, and it is strongly limited in deserts and polar regions.
Satellite estimates put Earth's total primary production at 104.9 petagrams of carbon per year, 56.4 on land and 48.5 in the oceans.
Human societies are part of Earth's primary production cycle but influence it disproportionately.

title: Gross and net primary production
article: Primary production#Gross primary production and net primary production

definition.text: Gross primary production is all the chemical energy producers capture in a given time; net primary production is what remains after they use some for their own respiration.

facts.text: Net primary production is what is available for producers' growth and reproduction, and so for herbivores to eat.
Net primary productivity equals gross primary productivity minus the carbon producers lose through cellular respiration.
Gross production is harder to measure than net, because respiration constantly uses up some of the sugars produced.
Estimates scaled up from eddy covariance measurements give a land gross primary production of 123±8 Gt of carbon per year for 1998-2005.

definition.text: The making of organic matter in the sea, carried out almost entirely by algae.

facts.text: It happens in the photic zone, a sunlit surface layer about 10-100 m thick.
Sinking particles constantly remove nutrients from the sunlit layer, which are replaced only when deeper water mixes or wells up.
Where wind-blown desert dust does not reach, as in the Southern and North Pacific oceans, lack of iron limits production, creating high-nutrient, low-chlorophyll regions.
